## A human progeria dataset

We'll be grabbing an RNA-Seq dataset from the data repository GEO. Geo stands for "Gene Expression Omnibus". You can read more about GEO here: 
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/info/overview.html

From GEO, I used the GSE206684_RAW.tar file. I downloaded it into GitHub using this code: wget -O data/progeria/GSE206684_RAW.tar "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/series/GSE206nnn/GSE206684/suppl/GSE206684_RAW.tar"
Then, I extracted the files using the tar command: tar -xvf data/progeria/GSE206684_RAW.tar and the files were in .tsv.gz format. 
Then, I wanted them in .tsv format, so to do this I entered *.tsv.gz 

The human progeria dataset has 11 individuals from the ages 2-20. The datasets contain skin samples from these individuals. The genotype is HGPS which stands for Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome. 
Progeria is basically a condition where rapid aging occurs. 
```

## Working with human progeria data

# Look at the first five rows of the first sample
read.delim(files[1], header = FALSE, nrows = 5)

# Check the file list
str(files)

# Check the first few gene counts
head(read.delim(files[1], header = FALSE))

# Combining the progeria samples so that it's not 11 separate files and they can be analyzed together. 
```{r combine_samples}
x <- readDGE(files, columns = c(1, 2))
dim(x)
head(x)
```
next, we want to take all the sample names and store them as column names and then repeat those column names so we can see them and verify that they are what we are looking for.
```{r whatsinaname}
samplenames <- basename(files)
samplenames
``` 

```{r brandnewname}

colnames(x) <- samplenames
colnames(x)

```
next, we want to take the rownames and store them as gene symbols. then, we want to look up information about the gene symbols, etc. in the human progeria data set. 
## Human Gene Annotation
```{r human_annotation}
gene_symbols <- rownames(x)

human_genes <- select(
  Homo.sapiens,
  keys = unique(gene_symbols),
  columns = c("ENTREZID", "TXNAME"),
  keytype = "SYMBOL"
)

head(human_genes)
```
we use c as the combine function to combine all the different ages information so it can be analyzed together. 
```{r sample_info}
sample_info <- data.frame(
  sample = basename(files),
  age = c(20, 14, 20, 10, 3, 2, 8, 17, 4, 8, 2)
)
```
making the pca plot
# PCA Analysis 
```{r PCA}
# Normalize the gene counts
x <- calcNormFactors(x)

# Convert counts to log values
logCPM <- cpm(x, log = TRUE, prior.count = 2)

# Perform PCA
pca <- prcomp(t(logCPM))

# Color samples by age group
sample_colors <- ifelse(sample_info$age <= 8, "blue", "red")

# Make the PCA plot
plot(pca$x[,1], pca$x[,2],
     col = sample_colors,
     pch = 19,
     xlab = "PC1",
     ylab = "PC2",
     main = "PCA of Progeria Samples by Age")

legend("topright",
       legend = c("Age 2–8", "Age 10–20"),
       col = c("blue", "red"),
       pch = 19)
```

## Differential Gene Expression
```{r differential_expression}
# Divide samples into younger and older groups
sample_info$age_group <- factor(
  ifelse(sample_info$age <= 8, "Younger", "Older"),
  levels = c("Younger", "Older")
)

# Create the analysis design
design <- model.matrix(~ age_group, data = sample_info)

# Run the differential expression analysis
x <- estimateDisp(x, design)
fit <- glmQLFit(x, design)
results <- glmQLFTest(fit, coef = 2)

# Display the top 20 differentially expressed genes
topTags(results, n = 20)
```

## Interpretation of Results
The PCA plot was done to investigate whether the younger age groups and older age groups showed a difference in gene expression. Because the adjusted p-values (FDR) are all greater than 0.05, there is not a signficant difference between the age groups and the gene expression. Based on the PCA plot, we can see that the age groups do cluster generally, however, not signifcantly based on the statistical analysis.
